plan_metadata.objective: Lead-lag (cross-correlation) analysis between state-level Zillow ZHVI trends and state unemployment-rate trends, 2010-01..2019-12, lags -24..+24 months, per-state strongest lag + ranking of relationships with |r| > 0.1.

inputs.path: Unemployment in America Per US State.csv

used_columns.Month: timestamp part (cast to int; raw file reads as int64, do NOT assume zero-padding)

used_columns.StateName: already 2-letter USPS -> state identifier for ZHVI
used_columns.RegionName: state full name (cross-check join key only)
used_columns.region/month columns matching r'^\\d{4}-: wide month columns, month-END labels, 291 columns 1996-01..2020-03

known_data_issues_and_mitigations.issue: Two non-state rows in unemployment ('Los Angeles County', 'New York city')
known_data_issues_and_mitigations.mitigation: drop explicitly before name->USPS mapping; do not rely on FIPS (FIPS not uniform width, reads as int64)

known_data_issues_and_mitigations.issue: Unemployment rate is a string with whitespace/commas and en-dash placeholder '–'
known_data_issues_and_mitigations.mitigation: astype(str).str.strip().str.replace(',','') then pd.to_numeric(errors='coerce'); NaNs expected only in 2025 (outside window)

known_data_issues_and_mitigations.issue: ZHVI date columns are month-END labels
known_data_issues_and_mitigations.mitigation: normalize every label to month start: pd.to_datetime(col).to_period('M').to_timestamp(); join to unemployment month-start dates (otherwise zero matches)
pandas.melt with id_vars=['RegionID','RegionName','RegionType','StateName'] over the 291 date columns, then drop NaN values

known_data_issues_and_mitigations.issue: Both files contain history outside the analysis window
known_data_issues_and_mitigations.mitigation: compute 12-month rolling stats on the full per-state monthly history (needed for a populated window at 2010-01), then subset the rolling outputs to 2010-01..2019-12
assert no duplicates after melt/filter; if present, keep mean and log

state_identifier_normalization.rule: unemployment State/Area (full names) -> USPS 2-letter via a 50-state + 'District of Columbia'->'DC' map; ZHVI uses StateName directly (already USPS)
state_identifier_normalization.cross_check: set(unemployment USPS) == set(ZHVI StateName); expected 51 / 51 matched, 0 unmatched on either side

timestamp_convention.rule: all timestamps = first day of the calendar month (pandas 'MS' / Period('M')->to_timestamp())
timestamp_convention.analysis_index: pd.date_range('2010-01-01','2019-12-01', freq='MS') -> 120 periods, identical for every state

pipeline_steps.name: load_and_clean_long_format
details: Read both files with the encodings above; restrict unemployment to Year between 1976 and max year (all years kept for rolling-window history).
Unemployment: keep [state_name, year, month, unemployment_rate], drop non-state rows, cast rate to numeric, build month_start date, map state -> USPS, drop any remaining NaN rate rows.
ZHVI: drop 'Unnamed: 0', melt wide->long (variable -> date label, value -> zhvi), coerce date labels to month_start, drop NaN zhvi, keep [state, month_start, zhvi] with state = StateName.
Build tidy frames: zhvi_long (state, month_start, ZHVI) and unemp_long (state, month_start, Unemployment_Rate); sort by (state, month_start).

pipeline_steps.name: zhvi_rolling_statistics
details: For each state, reindex ZHVI onto a gap-free monthly range from its first to last month, then compute Rolling_Mean = zhvi.rolling(window=12, min_periods=6).mean() and Rolling_Std = zhvi.rolling(window=12, min_periods=6).std().
min_periods=6 means the first 5 months of each state's history stay NaN; by 2010-01 every state has >= 168 prior months, so all 120 in-window months are populated.
Store ZHVI_Rolling_Mean and ZHVI_Rolling_Std.
qc: non-null count of ZHVI_Rolling_Mean inside 2010-01..2019-12 == 120 per state

pipeline_steps.name: unemployment_rolling_statistics
details: Identical treatment: per state gap-free monthly reindex, Unemployment_Rolling_Mean = rolling(window=12, min_periods=6).mean(), Unemployment_Rolling_Std = rolling(12, min_periods=6).std().
Unemployment history starts 1976-01 so the 2010-01..2019-12 window is fully populated.
qc: non-null count of Unemployment_Rolling_Mean inside window == 120 per state

pipeline_steps.name: cross_correlation_-24_+24
details: For each state: take ZHVI_Rolling_Mean and Unemployment_Rolling_Mean, reindex BOTH to pd.date_range('2010-01-01','2019-12-01', freq='MS'), then fill missing with .ffill().bfill() (forward fill first, then backward fill) exactly once, in that order.

For lag k in -24..+24: r(k) = Pearson corr( ZHVI[t] , Unemployment[t+k] ) over the overlapping pairs only (dropna on the pair); implemented as corr(zhvi_rm, unemp_rm.shift(-k)) so shift(-k) pulls the value from t+k onto t.
Sign convention: k<0 -> unemployment value taken from earlier months -> 'Unemployment leads ZHVI'; k>0 -> ZHVI leads; k==0 -> 'Synchronous'.
Require >= 48 overlapping observations per lag (120-|k| = 96..120 months is expected) and |r| <= 1; r is the normalized (mean/variance standardized) cross-correlation by construction.
qc: overlap counts equal 120-|k| when no ffill/bfill changes occurred; record min overlap
SIGN SELF-TEST: on synthetic data where unemployment leads ZHVI by 5 months, argmax|r| must land on lag -5 (and mirror test for +5) - assert before trusting real results
all 51 states produce 49 lag values, none NaN

pipeline_steps.name: strongest_lag_and_ranking
details: Per state: lag_star = argmax_k |r(k)|; correlation = r(lag_star); abs_correlation = |r(lag_star)|; relationship label derived from lag_star sign.
Tie-breaking (deterministic): smallest |lag| first, then smaller lag value; keeps results reproducible.
Rank states by abs_correlation descending; significant = abs_correlation > 0.1 (strict). significant_relationships_found = count of significant states.
qc: relationship label consistent with lag sign

pipeline_steps.name: write_output_json
details: top_10_relationships = first 10 rows of the ranked significant list (if fewer than 10 states exceed the threshold, emit all of them and note the shortfall in the plan/report rather than padding).
Each element: state, variable1='ZHVI_Rolling_Mean', variable2='Unemployment_Rolling_Mean', correlation (round 4), lag_months (int), abs_correlation (round 4), relationship.
summary_statistics computed over those top-10 rows: mean/max/min of correlation (signed, round 4) and mean of lag_months (round 1).
analysis_metadata: time_range='2010-01 to 2019-12', lag_range_months=[-24,24], correlation_threshold=0.1, window_size=12, total_states_analyzed=51 (int), significant_relationships_found (int).

top_10_relationships.relationship: one of ['Unemployment leads ZHVI','ZHVI leads Unemployment','Synchronous']

validation_checks: 51 states analyzed on both sides; 0 unmatched names after USPS mapping
120 monthly rows per state in the analysis index; 0 NaN after ffill+bfill for both rolling means
49 lag values (-24..24) per state; every correlation finite and within [-1,1]
sign-convention self-test on synthetic lagged series passes before final run
output.json JSON-parses, all required keys present, rounding rules applied
significant_relationships_found equals the number of states with abs_correlation > 0.1, and equals len(ranked significant list)
risks_and_notes: Pearson r on trending/autocorrelated rolling means is descriptive, not causal; correlations are expected to be strongly negative if ZHVI rises while unemployment falls (both de-trended only by rolling mean).
Only rolling MEAN series enter the correlation; rolling STD is computed as required by steps 2-3 but is not part of the correlation output.
Because ZHVI and unemployment are not differenced, level-trend correlation may dominate; interpret lags as lead-lag of smoothed levels, and state this caveat in the final report.
If >=10 states exceed threshold a top-10 slice is emitted; the full per-state lag table should still be saved as an intermediate artifact (e.g. state_lag_table.csv) for traceability.
